denoise: After one epoch, most Gaussian speckle is removed and the ten displayed test digits are already largely recognizable. By epoch five, backgrounds are cleaner and strokes are more continuous and sharply defined, especially in 1, 2, and 7. The reconstruction is still a smoothed estimate: the displayed 3 has a rounded, almost 8-like form, and the lower stroke of 5 remains broad; exact handwritten stroke widths are not recovered. On the same fixed 1,000-image MNIST test subset and the same sigma=0.5 corruption, MSE falls from 0.0118288 at epoch one to 0.00831475 at epoch five (a 29.7% decrease), while PSNR rises from 19.27 to 20.80 dB. The noisy inputs have MSE 0.250885, so the final reconstruction error is about 30.2 times smaller. Mean training MSE decreases from 0.0205639 in epoch one to 0.00824019 in epoch five across all 60,000 training images per epoch. These are reconstruction measurements; no digit-classification accuracy was measured.
denoise_ood: The fixed digits remain mostly legible from sigma=0.0 through 0.6. At sigma=0 the network still smooths and slightly reshapes clean strokes, so it is not an identity map: its test MSE is 0.00335856 even though the input error is zero. Increasing noise to 0.8 introduces false strokes and shape changes, particularly in the displayed 1, 2, and 7. At sigma=1.0 the displayed 1 becomes fragmented and several digits acquire extra branches; some large silhouettes, including 0 and 6, remain recognizable. For the fixed 1,000-image test subset, output MSE at sigma=0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 is respectively 0.00335856, 0.00404778, 0.00631606, 0.00831475, 0.0113586, 0.0230761, and 0.0414820. Thus the model suppresses substantial noise beyond its training level, but reconstruction error and visible artifacts increase as the corruption grows. Only visualization pixels are clipped; these numerical errors use the unbounded model predictions and noisy tensors.
pure_noise: At epochs 1 and 5, the 40 fixed noise inputs produce very similar blurry gray ovals with overlapping 0/8-like loops. They do not form a diverse set of recognizable digits 0–9. By epoch 5, differences between outputs are even smaller: mean pixel variance across samples falls from 0.0002846 to 0.0000459, while MSE to the empirical training-image centroid falls from 0.0004328 to 0.0000707. Training MSE changes from 0.07319 to 0.06738. Because each Gaussian input is independent of its target digit, minimizing expected squared error favors the same mean training image for every input; the observed overlapping strokes are consistent with that conditional-mean solution.
time_flow: Using the same 40 starting noise tensors at every saved epoch, epoch 1 mostly produces disconnected strokes and partial loops. By epoch 5, many samples form recognizable digits, including 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9-like shapes, with varied stroke thickness and slant. Epoch 10 further cleans up several loops and junctions, although some samples remain ambiguous or fragmented; the model does not have a requested class to disambiguate them. Mean velocity-training MSE decreases from 0.18320 at epoch 1 to 0.10159 at epoch 5 and 0.09321 at epoch 10. The visual improvement is substantial relative to epoch 1 and more modest between epochs 5 and 10. Unlike the pure-noise regression baseline, flow sampling generates diverse shapes instead of repeatedly returning the average training image.
class_flow: The class-conditioned model produces the requested digit categories after one epoch, but several 4s, 5s, 6s, 7s, and 9s contain gaps or detached strokes. By epoch 5, the four examples in each column are readily recognizable as the requested class. Epoch 10 keeps that label agreement and further regularizes loops and joins, while preserving visible variation in slant, width, and stroke thickness. The class-conditioned grids are more consistently legible than the time-only epoch-10 grid. This is a visual comparison of the saved 40 samples, not a measured classifier accuracy or a guarantee about all generated images. Class dropout is 0.1, and sampling uses 300 Euler steps with guidance gamma=5.
class_flow_no_scheduler: Removing the scheduler while lowering Adam’s fixed learning rate from the scheduled run’s initial 0.01 to a constant 0.001 preserves the quality of this fixed 40-sample comparison. Both epoch-10 grids contain four recognizable examples of each requested digit, with similar variation in stroke thickness and slant. The constant-rate model has slightly different stroke shapes, including broader crossbars on some 4s, but no clear overall loss of legibility. Final mean training MSE is 0.08459 without scheduling versus 0.08480 with scheduling, a difference of about 0.25%; this small difference is not evidence of a general advantage. The lower constant rate compensates by keeping updates modest throughout training. In this run it also gives a lower first-epoch loss (0.13807 versus 0.17001), so slower early convergence was not observed. Architecture, initialization seed, 60,000-image training split, epoch shuffles, sampling noise, 300 Euler steps, and guidance gamma=5 are matched.
